hook: Zoom in far enough on a smooth curve and it looks straight. That is why the ground looks flat even though Earth is round. Near a point, a differentiable function is almost its tangent line, and that line gives quick, good estimates. Knowing whether such an estimate is too high or too low is a classic free-response point.

figure.caption: The tangent line to $\sqrt{x}$ at $x = 4$ gives $L(7) = 2.75$, slightly above $\sqrt{7}$: the graph is concave down, so the line lies above it.

chain.cause: Near $x = a$, a differentiable graph is nearly straight
chain.effect: it is close to its tangent line $L(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x - a)$
$f(x) \approx f(a) + f'(a)(x - a)$, the tangent line approximation

chain.cause: If $f'' > 0$ between $a$ and $x$, the graph is concave up and lies above the line
If $f'' < 0$ there, the graph is concave down and lies below the line

ideas: The linearization at $a$: $L(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x - a)$. Use the point closest to where you estimate.
Concave up ($f'' > 0$): tangent line below the graph, underestimate. Concave down ($f'' < 0$): overestimate.
Justify with the concavity on the interval between $a$ and $x$, not with the sign of $f'$.
The closer $x$ is to $a$, the better the approximation.

misconception.wrong: The tangent line approximation overestimates because $f$ is increasing.
misconception.right: Whether $f$ increases decides which way the line slopes, not which side of the graph it is on. Concavity decides: concave down means overestimate, concave up means underestimate.

summary: Near $x = a$, $f(x) \approx L(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x - a)$. The tangent line lies below a concave up graph ($f'' > 0$), giving an underestimate, and above a concave down graph ($f'' < 0$), giving an overestimate. The estimate is best close to $a$.
